source: Yeager et al. (2019) A national experiment reveals where a growth mindset improves achievement
finding: Pre-registered national RCT of a short online growth-mindset intervention. Lower-achieving ninth graders got slightly higher core-course GPA.
numbers: N=12,490 students, 65 US public schools, individually randomized. Lower achievers n=6,320: B=0.10 grade points (95% CI 0.04-0.16), SMD 0.11, p=.001. Same B=0.10 for math and science GPA.
limits: Effect is on lower achievers only (pre-registered); under one hour of treatment; small in absolute terms.
agent_relevance: Even the best-run mindset effect is about 0.1 SD. A mindset-style instruction in a scaffold should be expected to give small average gains.

source: Yeager et al. (2019) A national experiment reveals where a growth mindset improves achievement
finding: Intervention cut the rate of D/F grades among lower achievers and raised advanced math course taking.
numbers: D/F rate fell from 46% to 41% (relative risk reduction 11%). Advanced math (algebra II+) in grade 10: 33% to 36% (+3 points, 95% CI 0.01-0.04, n=6,690, k=41); +4 points in top 25% of schools, +2 points in the rest.
limits: Course-taking effect was larger in high-achieving schools, opposite of the GPA pattern; a GPA-only analysis would have hidden it.
agent_relevance: Effects can show up in choice behaviour (taking harder tasks) rather than raw accuracy. Measure task selection, not only scores.

source: Yeager et al. (2019) A national experiment reveals where a growth mindset improves achievement
finding: Moderator: the effect depended on school peer norms. Where peers valued challenge-seeking, the intervention worked more.
numbers: Intervention x challenge-seeking norm interaction for lower achievers B=0.11 (95% CI 0.01-0.21), z=2.18, n=6,320, k=65. Intervention x student prior-achievement (lower-achiever) interaction B=0.09 (95% CI 0.01-0.17), p=.034, n=12,490. Norm measured from control students' choice of challenging math problems (out of 8).
quote: the intervention changed grades when peer norms aligned with the messages of the intervention
limits: Interaction p-values are modest and CIs wide, though moderators were pre-registered.
agent_relevance: Same prompt, different context, different result. An agent instruction needs a supportive context (tools, retries, verification) or it is empty exhortation.

source: Yeager et al. (2022) Teacher mindsets help explain where a growth-mindset intervention does and doesn't work
finding: Follow-up on the national study: the intervention raised math grades only in classes of teachers with growth mindsets.
numbers: 9,167 records, 223 math teachers. Fixed-mindset teachers (-1 SD): CATE -.02 [-.074,.038], p=.531. Growth-mindset teachers (+1 SD): CATE .11 [.046,.167], p<.001. Interaction b=0.09 [0.026,0.150], p=.005. Student mindset shift d=0.37 regardless of teacher.
quote: classroom needed to 'support, or at least permit' the mindset
limits: Teacher mindset was measured, not randomized; causal role untested. Mediation not tested.
agent_relevance: The belief change in the learner (d=0.37) did not by itself help. The environment must permit using it. A prompt may change stated stance, but performance needs a scaffold that rewards persistence.

source: Yeager et al. (2022) Teacher mindsets help explain where a growth-mindset intervention does and doesn't work
finding: Robustness and subgroup results in growth-mindset classrooms; teacher-level and school-level variation both large.
numbers: Growth-teacher CATE: .13 for prior lower achievers, .14 for students without straight As, .10 with school moderators added. Baseline fixed-mindset students gained 0.16 GPA (95% CI .079-.234) in growth classrooms. Teacher-level effects correlated r=.55 with teacher mindset (Bayesian causal forest). Variation: teacher about 47%, school about 49%.
limits: Observational moderator; confounds (pedagogical knowledge, fluid intelligence, implicit bias) did not remove the interaction but cannot be fully ruled out.
agent_relevance: Heterogeneity is large. Report effects by context, never one average.

source: Sisk et al. (2018) To what extent and under what circumstances are growth mind-sets important to academic achievement? Two meta-analyses
finding: Meta-analysis 1: the link between holding a growth mindset and achievement is weak.
numbers: k=273 effect sizes, 129 studies, 162 samples, N=365,915. Average r=.10 (95% CI .08-.13). 157 of 273 (58%) not significantly different from zero. Children r=.19, adolescents r=.15, adults r=.02 (CI -.005 to .05).
limits: Correlational. Mindset is self-reported; achievement measures vary.
agent_relevance: The popular claim (mindset predicts success) is r about .1. Do not build an agent design on it.

source: Sisk et al. (2018) To what extent and under what circumstances are growth mind-sets important to academic achievement? Two meta-analyses
finding: Meta-analysis 2: mindset interventions had weak effects overall.
numbers: k=43 effect sizes, 29 studies, 38 samples, N=57,155. Adolescents d=0.08 (95% CI -0.01 to 0.17, p=.090); adults d=0.08 (95% CI -0.02 to 0.17, p=.123).
quote: Overall effects were weak for both meta-analyses.
limits: Few high-quality trials; heterogeneity high; many small studies.
agent_relevance: Prior for any mindset manipulation of an agent: near-zero average effect.

source: Sisk et al. (2018) To what extent and under what circumstances are growth mind-sets important to academic achievement? Two meta-analyses
finding: Moderators: low-SES and academically at-risk students may benefit more, as the theory predicts, but the evidence is mixed.
numbers: Mindset-achievement r=.17 (CI .10-.23) for low-SES vs r=.12 (CI .09-.16) for middle and higher SES. By risk: low r=.11, moderate r=.11, high r=.08 (CI -.04 to .21). In the intervention meta-analysis, at-risk status was not a significant moderator: Q(2)=0.67, p=.715.
limits: Subgroup counts are small; the two moderator results point in slightly different directions.
agent_relevance: Largest gains tend to go where baseline is weakest. A weak base model may gain more from scaffolding than a strong one.

source: Macnamara & Burgoyne (2023) Do growth mindset interventions impact students' academic achievement? Psychological Bulletin (figures from secondary search summaries; paper not opened)
finding: Larger sceptical meta-analysis. Authors conclude apparent effects come from design flaws, reporting problems and bias.
numbers: 63 studies, N=97,672. Overall d=0.05 (95% CI 0.02-0.09). Studies that changed mindset d=0.04. Highest-quality studies d=0.02. Not significant after publication-bias adjustment (as reported).
limits: Numbers taken from summaries, not read in the paper. Methods disputed by Tipton et al.
agent_relevance: Strong sceptical prior: treat mindset effects as small unless a preregistered replication shows otherwise.

source: Tipton et al. (2023) Why meta-analyses of growth mindset and other interventions should follow best practices for examining heterogeneity (Psychological Bulletin commentary)
finding: Re-analysis of the sceptical meta-analysis's data with a multilevel model gives a larger, positive, heterogeneous effect, strongest for at-risk groups.
numbers: k=122 effect sizes. Overall 0.09 SD (p<.001). At-risk groups 0.15 SD (p<.001). Heterogeneity tau2+omega2=0.16, about twice the 0.07 from the traditional approach. 95% prediction interval -0.22 to 0.40. Quality-restricted sensitivity: overall 0.05 (p=.004), at-risk 0.12 (p=.01). Burnette et al. report 0.09 overall, 0.16 at-risk, interval -0.08 to 0.35.
limits: Self-described exploratory; authors do not claim a final verdict; authors are not neutral (Yeager co-author).
agent_relevance: The fair summary: mean about 0.05-0.09 SD, but true effects range from negative to +0.4 by context. Make context-conditional claims only.

source: Tipton et al. (2023) Why meta-analyses of growth mindset and other interventions should follow best practices for examining heterogeneity (Psychological Bulletin commentary)
finding: Methodological critique of the sceptical meta-analysis: one effect per study, one moderator at a time, ad hoc quality score, publication-bias tests unreliable under heterogeneity.
numbers: Peru study (over 54,000 students, 799 schools) had ten varying effects collapsed to one d=0.02. Footnote 5: the 'high-quality' subgroup result was an artifact of miscoded studies. Egger test was significant (z=3.47) in the Open Science Collaboration data even though no publication bias existed.
limits: Coding disputes between two author groups remain unresolved.
agent_relevance: Averaging over tasks hides context-specific wins and losses. Log per-task results in our own evaluations.

source: Li & Bates (2019) Does growth mindset improve children's IQ, educational attainment or response to setbacks? (from memory, not opened)
finding: Independent test with Chinese school children reported no effect of a growth-mindset intervention on IQ, grades or response to setbacks.
numbers: About 600 children across two studies (exact N not verified). Null effects with active controls.
limits: Memory-based; verify before citing. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Another null: stated belief shift without behaviour change.

source: Foliano et al. (2019) Changing Mindsets, EEF evaluation report (from memory, not opened)
finding: Large UK cluster RCT of a growth-mindset teaching programme found no measurable effect on KS2 reading and maths.
numbers: About 100 schools and 5,000 pupils; effect reported as zero months' progress (exact figures not verified).
limits: Memory-based; check report. Different programme from the US online module.
agent_relevance: Independent, large, null result. Weighs against lightweight mindset messaging at scale.

source: Bahnik & Vranka (2017) Growth mindset is not associated with scholastic aptitude in a large sample of university applicants (from memory, not opened)
finding: In a large sample of university applicants, self-reported growth mindset was essentially unrelated to scholastic aptitude scores.
numbers: Sample of several thousand; correlation near zero (exact value not verified).
limits: Memory-based; applicant sample is range-restricted.
agent_relevance: Belief in malleability does not by itself predict capability.

source: Mueller & Dweck (1998) Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance (from memory, not opened)
finding: Founding praise studies with fifth graders: praise for intelligence led to challenge avoidance, lower persistence after failure and more score misreporting than praise for effort.
numbers: Six experiments, roughly 400 children. About 38% vs 13% score inflation (intelligence vs effort praise) in one study (from memory, verify).
limits: Memory-based. Independent replication of the praise effects is mixed; not verified here.
agent_relevance: Wording of feedback shapes later behaviour. In an agent, reward or critique wording may bias toward easy goals.

source: Blackwell, Trzesniewski & Dweck (2007) Implicit theories of intelligence predict achievement across an adolescent transition (from memory, not opened)
finding: Founding field studies. Study 1: mindset predicted math grade trajectory over two years in 373 seventh graders. Study 2: an eight-session workshop reversed the grade decline vs control.
numbers: Study 1 N=373; Study 2 about 91 students (from memory, verify).
limits: Memory-based. Small intervention sample; later large trials gave about 0.1 SD.
agent_relevance: Pattern: small early study, big effect; large later study, small effect. Expect shrinkage for agent mindset prompts too.

source: Li et al. (2023) Large Language Models Understand and Can Be Enhanced by Emotional Stimuli (EmotionPrompt)
finding: Appending emotional or motivational sentences to prompts raised scores on benchmarks across six LLMs. One stimulus (EP08) is growth-mindset flavoured.
numbers: Headline: 8.00% relative gain on 24 Instruction Induction tasks, 115% relative on 21 BIG-Bench tasks. Models: Flan-T5-Large, Vicuna, Llama 2, BLOOM, ChatGPT, GPT-4. Human study 106 participants: 10.9% average gain on performance, truthfulness, responsibility.
quote: EP08: Embrace challenges as opportunities for growth. Each obstacle you overcome brings you closer to success.
limits: Headline uses best stimulus per task; see next line. BIG-Bench base scores are low so relative gains are inflated.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue of mindset messaging. Test growth-framed stimuli as a cheap ablation, not as a core operator.

source: Li et al. (2023) Large Language Models Understand and Can Be Enhanced by Emotional Stimuli (EmotionPrompt)
finding: Table 1 shows the average stimulus is close to no gain; the headline comes from picking the best stimulus per task.
numbers: Instruction Induction zero-shot averages over 6 models: Original 51.65, +Ours (avg) 51.98, +Ours (max) 55.24, +Zero-shot-CoT 46.74. GPT-4: Original 80.75, Ours avg 78.96 (lower), Ours max 81.60. Flan-T5: 25.25 / 22.93 / 25.53. Vicuna 44.91 / 50.56 / 54.49. Within Instruction Induction EP02 ('very important to my career') best; best beats worst by 6.06%.
limits: The max row is an oracle selection on the test tasks. Zero-shot only for BIG-Bench.
agent_relevance: Average of random motivational phrases is about +0.3 points. Gains need selection on a dev set, and strong models (GPT-4) may lose.

source: Wang et al. (2024) NegativePrompt: Leveraging Psychology for Large Language Models Enhancement via Negative Emotional Stimuli
finding: Negative emotional stimuli (appended to prompts) also raised scores, which suggests the content of the stimulus matters less than the extra tokens or attention shift.
numbers: Reported relative improvements of 12.89% on Instruction Induction and 46.25% on BIG-Bench.
limits: Same group and benchmarks as EmotionPrompt; same best-of selection caveat likely applies (not checked in detail); no external replication seen here.
agent_relevance: If both positive and negative framings help, the mechanism is probably not mindset. Do not credit a psychological account.

source: Yin et al. (2024) Should We Respect LLMs? A Cross-Lingual Study on the Influence of Prompt Politeness on LLM Performance
finding: Politeness level in prompts changes performance, but non-monotonically and by language. Rude prompts often hurt; very polite ones do not reliably help.
numbers: Eight politeness levels from high to low in English, Chinese and Japanese; one task checked here was summarisation (ROUGE-L and BERTScore stable across politeness, output length varies strongly). Best level differs by language. (Exact per-level scores not extracted.)
quote: impolite prompts often result in poor performance, but overly polite language does not guarantee better outcomes
limits: Older models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama 2, ChatGLM3 era); effects vary by model and task.
agent_relevance: Tone sensitivity exists but is model- and language-specific. Fix one tone in the scaffold and do not tune it per task.

source: Dobariya & Kumar (2025) Mind Your Tone: Investigating How Prompt Politeness Affects LLM Accuracy
finding: Reverse result on GPT-4o: rude prompts scored higher than polite ones.
numbers: 50 multiple-choice questions x 5 tones = 250 prompts. Accuracy from 80.8% (Very Polite) to 84.8% (Very Rude); paired t-tests, Very Polite vs Neutral p=.0024 and vs Rude p=0.0441 (as extracted).
limits: Tiny item set (50), one model, single-run per tone, preliminary short paper; 4-point spread is about 2 questions per 50 at the item level.
agent_relevance: Reversal across model generations means tone effects do not transfer. Evidence against hard-coding any affective framing.

source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick & Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 3: I'll pay you or I'll kill you -- but will you care?
finding: Large test of tips and threats in prompts: no significant aggregate effect on hard benchmarks, but big per-question swings.
numbers: GPQA (N=4,950 trials) and MMLU-Pro (N=2,500 trials); 25 trials per question; models Gemini 1.5 Flash, Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o4-mini. Aggregate effects not significant; per-question changes up to +36 and -35 percentage points.
quote: Threatening or tipping a model generally has no significant effect on benchmark performance.
limits: Academic benchmarks only, subset of models.
agent_relevance: Best-controlled null on motivational prompts. Folk effects average out; use verification and sampling, not pep talks.

source: Kestin et al. (2025) AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting
finding: Randomized crossover trial: a structured AI tutor (built on pedagogy best practice) beat in-class active learning, and students reported more engagement and motivation.
numbers: N=194 Harvard physics students, crossover. Median post-test 4.5 (AI, n=142) vs 3.5 (class, n=174), pre-test 2.75. Linear-model effect size 0.63 SD; quantile estimate 0.73-1.3 SD; rank-sum z=-5.6. Students learned more in less time (median 49 min on AI lesson).
limits: One course, one topic area, novices, short-term post-test, measures of motivation are self-report. Design embeds many features, so no single factor (such as growth-mindset messaging) is isolated.
agent_relevance: Motivation outcomes in LLM tutoring come from structure (scaffolding, feedback), not from mindset slogans. Supports scaffold-over-exhortation.

source: Kestin et al. (2025) AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting
finding: The paper names promoting a growth mindset as an expected tutoring feature and notes generic chatbots do not follow such practices; earlier unguided ChatGPT use showed limited reflection or lower performance.
numbers: Cites Krupp et al. (2023) limited reflection without guidance, and Forero (2023) lower performance when AI interaction lacked structure.
limits: Citation context only; the growth-mindset component was not tested separately.
agent_relevance: No LLM study found here that isolates a growth-mindset component. That is an open gap.

source: Burnette et al. (2023) growth mindset multilevel meta-regression, as summarised in Tipton et al. (2023)
finding: A second re-analysis found a positive overall effect and a larger effect for at-risk groups, with a narrower prediction interval than Tipton's re-fit.
numbers: Overall 0.09 SD; at-risk 0.16 SD; 95% prediction interval -0.08 to 0.35 SD.
limits: Seen only through the Tipton commentary; the original paper was not opened. Quality measures partly non-standard.
agent_relevance: Across analyses the mean is about 0.05-0.09 SD with a wide band. Plan for small, variable effects.
